project.title: Workplace Automation and Filipino Workers
project.titleSub: Evaluating Reskilling, Job Redesign, and Career Conversion
project.position: I support the continued use of workplace automation, because the evidence so far shows it is changing Filipino jobs more than erasing them, and it can raise productivity and open up higher value work. But exposure is concentrated in IT-BPM, in roles held by women and young workers, and in NCR and nearby regions, and readiness is uneven. So automation should be paired with deliberate support for the workers whose roles are changing, designed into the transition rather than offered after people have already lost ground.

solutions.name: Government-funded reskilling and upskilling
solutions.what: 740 million pesos to train up to 340,000 participants over three years in digital and AI skills, including near-hire individuals and college students.
solutions.who: National government funds it, the industry association helps steer it.
solutions.status: Approved and funded, set to start in the second half of 2025. Not a programme with published results.
solutions.targetPopulation: Workers already employed in IT-BPM, with the programme also open to near-hire individuals and college students. Up to 340,000 places over three years.
detail: IBPAP aligns programme strategies with TESDA and DICT.
The target group includes people close to being hired as well as college students, so it covers both current and incoming workers.

Training supply was expanded separately by a TESDA memorandum with LinkedIn in May 2025, opening more than 23,000 LinkedIn Learning courses to TESDA stakeholders as part of an effort aimed at BPO workers.
Republic Act No. 11962 gives the legal basis, covering skilling, upskilling and reskilling with an emphasis on lifelong learning.

solutions.name: Employer-led job redesign
solutions.what: Grants for enterprises to work with pre-approved consultants on redesigning work processes, tasks and responsibilities.
solutions.who: The employer decides, government subsidises the consultancy.
solutions.status: The Workforce Singapore page stated that the grant would end on 31 December 2025. From March 2026 it was replaced by the SkillsFuture Workforce Development Grant (Job Redesign+), which funds up to 70 percent of job redesign costs for SMEs and up to 50 percent for larger firms, capped at 150,000 Singapore dollars per enterprise.
solutions.targetPopulation: Enterprises rather than individuals. The employer applies, and the workers affected are whoever holds the redesigned roles.
detail: Under the original grant, firms could claim up to 30,000 Singapore dollars for consultancy, with a higher funding share for SMEs than for larger firms.
The original grant was administered by the Singapore National Employers Federation on Workforce Singapore’s behalf.
The successor grant extends support beyond consultancy to capability building in job redesign, and is open to enterprises operating in Singapore with at least three local employees.

In the Philippines, industry reporting describes firms using AI to augment staff and creating roles such as AI trainers, prompt engineers and AI ethicists. That is related practice rather than a formal job-redesign programme.

solutions.name: Place-and-train career conversion
solutions.what: A jobseeker is hired into a new growth role by a participating company, which then provides on-the-job or industry-recognised training.
solutions.who: The employer hires first, government supports the training period.
solutions.status: An existing Singapore programme with a published impact evaluation.
solutions.targetPopulation: Jobseekers moving into a growth role in a new sector or occupation, hired by a participating employer before they are fully trained.
detail: The worker is placed with a participating employer and then trained into the new role on the job, which is why it is called place-and-train rather than train-and-place.
The employer carries the person while the training happens, with government support.
The published evaluation compared participants against control groups.

The paper carries a disclaimer that the views are the authors’ own rather than official agency positions, so the figures should be read as a government-published study rather than a formal agency position.

solutions.name: JobStart Philippines
solutions.what: Life skills training, technical training and a paid internship with a partner employer, for young jobseekers.
solutions.who: DOLE funds it through the Bureau of Local Employment, PESOs deliver it, employers host the internship.
solutions.status: Institutionalised nationwide by Republic Act No. 10869, approved 29 June 2016. Running now.
solutions.targetPopulation: Filipinos aged 18 to 24 at registration who are not employed, studying or in training, with no work experience or under one year of it.
detail: The Act sets the stages: ten days of life skills training, up to three months of technical training with a TESDA-accredited provider or the employer, and an internship of up to three months or 600 hours.

The Act requires the employer to pay an internship stipend of at least 75 percent of the prevailing minimum wage where the establishment is located. It provides a daily training allowance without fixing the amount, which DOLE sets.

DOLE publishes the current amounts: 400 pesos a day during training, and a partner employer grant covering training costs and the allowance plus 1,500 pesos per trainee per month for administrative costs.

Section 5 restricts it to Filipinos aged 18 to 24 at registration who are not employed, studying or in training, with no work experience or less than one year of it. Seventeen year olds may register if they will be 18 by the technical training stage.

solutions.name: Portable individual training credit
solutions.what: Training money given to the individual rather than to a programme or an employer.
solutions.who: Government funds it, the worker chooses the course.
solutions.status: Running. Take-up of the one-off top-up is documented in a parliamentary reply.
solutions.targetPopulation: Individual Singaporeans by age rather than by occupation or sector, which is what makes the funding portable across jobs and employment status.
detail: Singaporeans receive an Opening Credit of 500 dollars at age 25 and a Mid-Career Credit of 4,000 dollars at age 40, neither of which expires.
A separate one-off 500 dollar top-up was given in 2020 to those aged 25 and above, expiring at the end of 2025.
As at end-September 2025, close to 800,000 Singaporeans, about 3 in 10 eligible people, had used the one-off top-up. Mid-career workers aged 40 to 60 made up close to half of users.
Relevant to the Philippines because the funding follows the person rather than the job, which in principle reaches workers outside IT-BPM and outside formal employment.

smart.name: Conversion completion
smart.definition: The share of workers entering the track who finish the full training and placement cycle.
smart.source: PESO monthly monitoring reports, which JobStart already requires
smart.owner: PESO, consolidated by the Bureau of Local Employment
smart.assumption: Completion is not employment. It shows the cycle ran, not that it worked.
smart.objective: Establish whether workers who enter the track actually complete it, so that drop-out is visible early rather than at the end of a cohort.
smart.targetGroup: Workers entering a first conversion cohort, drawn from automation-exposed roles.
smart.baseline: No Philippine baseline exists. I found no published completion rate for JobStart or for the IT-BPM reskilling commitment, so the first cohort would set the baseline.

smart.name: Placement retention
smart.definition: The share still employed in the converted role six months after completion.
smart.method: Employer reports, cross-checked against contribution records
smart.source: Employer returns to PESO, with SSS record matching where it can be arranged
smart.assumption: Employer self-reporting can be optimistic, and record matching would need a data sharing arrangement.
smart.objective: Test whether a conversion place turns into lasting employment rather than a short placement that ends when support does.
smart.targetGroup: Workers who complete the conversion cycle and enter the converted role.
smart.baseline: No Philippine baseline exists. Singapore reported a retention effect of 3.9 percentage points against control groups, but that is a measured effect there, not a starting point here.

smart.name: Wage change
smart.definition: Wage in the converted role against wage in the prior role. Singapore measured this, so it is the fairest test of whether the model transfers.
smart.target: No real wage decrease for at least 80 percent of completers
smart.method: Compare payroll at entry and at 12 months
smart.source: Payroll data supplied by participating employers
smart.assumption: Covers only formally employed participants, and says nothing about workers who never entered.
smart.objective: Check that converting role does not cost a worker income, which is the risk that would make the track not worth entering.
smart.targetGroup: Completers who were in paid work before entering the track.
smart.baseline: Each participant’s own wage at entry serves as the baseline, recorded from payroll at the point of entry. No national baseline is needed or claimed.

smart.name: Employer participation
smart.definition: The number of firms offering conversion places. The model fails if employers do not hire first.
smart.target: 30 participating firms in a first cohort
smart.source: Agreements held by the Bureau of Local Employment
smart.assumption: Counts firms, not the quality of the roles they offer.
smart.objective: Establish whether employers will hire before training is complete, which is the single assumption the whole model rests on.
smart.targetGroup: Employers in sectors with high automation exposure, starting with IT-BPM.
smart.baseline: No Philippine baseline exists, because no comparable place-and-train scheme runs here. JobStart partner employer counts are not comparable, since those are internship hosts rather than conversion employers.

smart.name: Reach into exposed groups
smart.definition: The share of places going to the groups the ILO identifies as most exposed: women, young entry-level workers and NCR-based roles.
smart.method: Compare intake records against the ILO Philippines brief
smart.source: PESO intake records and the ILO brief
smart.assumption: The ILO figure is exposure, not displacement, so it is a reference point rather than a demand estimate.
smart.objective: Check that places reach the groups the exposure evidence identifies, rather than the easiest candidates to recruit.
smart.targetGroup: Women, young entry-level workers, and workers in NCR, Central Luzon and Calabarzon.

smart.name: Worker-reported outcome
smart.definition: Whether participants say the conversion improved their security and prospects. Worker acceptability was unmeasured in everything I reviewed.
smart.target: Establish a baseline in the first cohort rather than set a pass mark
smart.source: Survey at completion and at six months
smart.assumption: Self-reported. A first round sets a baseline and cannot be a pass or fail.
smart.objective: Record whether participants themselves judge the conversion to have improved their security and prospects, since no source I reviewed measures worker acceptance at all.
smart.targetGroup: Participants who complete the cycle, surveyed individually.
smart.baseline: None exists anywhere in the sources reviewed. Worker acceptability is unmeasured, which is why this indicator sets a baseline in the first cohort instead of a pass mark.

proposal.name: A Philippine place-and-train career conversion track
proposal.claim: A proposal, not an existing programme. Nothing in my sources says any agency or employer has agreed to it.

mechanism.d: A worker is taken on by a participating employer into a new growth role before being fully trained.
The employer provides on-the-job or industry-recognised training for that role, registered with TESDA under the EBET framework.
Government supports the employer while the conversion runs, so the worker’s income does not stop.

missing: I found no Philippine funding line for career conversion itself.
I found no agency that matches an automation-displaced worker to a conversion role.
No existing scheme replaces income during a mid-career transition.

haveLegal.t: RA 11962, Trabaho Para sa Bayan Act
haveLegal.d: Establishes a National Employment Master Plan. Section 4(b) covers skilling, upskilling and reskilling with an emphasis on lifelong learning; 4(c) encourages private sector skills transfer; 6(c) requires analysis of the employment situation.

Institutionalises enterprise-based education and training. Section 6 makes both new labour force entrants and employed workers eligible, and Section 4(i) covers enterprise upskilling for existing employees. TESDA is the primary implementing agency.
Live funding attached to the reskilling mandate, targeting up to 340,000 participants, including near-hire individuals and college students, set to start in the second half of 2025.

haveOps.d: RA 12063 Section 20 gives an additional deduction of 50 percent of actual training expenses through 31 December 2027, rising to 75 percent from 1 January 2028, capped at the lower of 5 percent of total direct labour expenses or 25 million pesos a year.

JobStart already does PESO intake and assessment, TESDA-accredited or employer-delivered technical training, a paid internship with a partner employer, a daily allowance set by DOLE, an employer grant, insurance and monthly monitoring.
TESDA opened more than 23,000 LinkedIn Learning courses to its stakeholders as part of an effort aimed at BPO workers.

adaptation.v: Workers already in automation-exposed roles, rather than JobStart’s 18 to 24 year old new entrants. RA 12063 Section 6 already makes employed workers eligible for enterprise-based training, so the training side needs no new eligibility rule.
PESO intake and assessment, as JobStart already does, with referral from employers who are automating roles.
Employer-delivered or TVI-partnered training registered with TESDA under the EBET framework.

A training allowance and stipend on the JobStart pattern, with the amount set for this group. This is the part no existing Philippine scheme provides for mid-career workers, and it is the core of the proposal.
The RA 12063 Section 20 training-expense deduction, which already exists in law, alongside a JobStart-style grant covering part of the allowance.
The existing IT-BPM reskilling commitment, at least for a first cohort in the sector where exposure is highest.
DOLE and PESOs to deliver, TESDA for standards and EBET registration, DICT and IBPAP for demand signals. None has been approached or has agreed to this.

resources: PESO staff time for intake, matching and monthly monitoring
TESDA-registered enterprise training programmes mapped to converted roles
Employers willing to open conversion posts
financial: A training allowance and stipend on the JobStart pattern, set for this group
The RA 12063 Section 20 deduction, which is already law rather than a new ask
Drawn from the existing IT-BPM commitment, so no new appropriation is assumed
depends: Employers hiring before training is complete
An income-support rule for mid-career trainees, which does not exist today
Funding continuing past a three-year commitment
benefits: Workers keep earning while their role changes
Employers fill growth roles from people they would otherwise let go
Outcomes get measured instead of assumed, which no Philippine option does now
verified: The 740 million peso commitment and its 2025 start
RA 11962, RA 10869 and RA 12063, each checked against the source text
JobStart’s stages, allowances, employer grant and eligibility rules
Singapore’s place-and-train design and its control-group results
ILO exposure figures for the Philippines and ASEAN
proposed: Combining EBET training with JobStart placement and stipend mechanics
Drawing on the IT-BPM funding for a first cohort
Every SMART target on this site
No agency has approved this, no budget is allocated, and no pilot results exist

proposalCriteria.label: Sustainability
proposalCriteria.body: It runs on machinery that already exists in law and in practice, which is why I chose this adaptation over building something new. RA 12063 in particular gives the training side a standing legal framework with a legislated employer incentive. The weakness is that the cash would come from a three-year commitment rather than a permanent facility.

proposalCriteria.label: Impact
proposalCriteria.verdict: High in principle, narrow at first
proposalCriteria.body: It keeps income in place during the transition, which none of the other four do. But a first cohort in IT-BPM would still reach a small fraction of the 12.7 million exposed workers.

proposalCriteria.label: Feasibility
proposalCriteria.verdict: Moderate, and better than I first judged
proposalCriteria.body: RA 12063 removes the eligibility obstacle I previously treated as the main barrier, because employed workers are already eligible for enterprise-based training and the employer deduction is already law. What remains missing is an income-support rule for mid-career trainees and a matching function for displaced workers.

proposalCriteria.label: Effectiveness
proposalCriteria.body: The wage and retention results are Singapore results. The Philippine version would have to earn its own numbers, which is what the SMART measures are for.

exposureByRegion.note: Around two in five jobs exposed

exposureNotes.v: Women face double the rate of exposure of men, because they are concentrated in high-exposure occupations. Women with advanced education face particularly high disruption potential.
Overall youth exposure is slightly lower than adult exposure, but young people are more likely to work in occupations at greater displacement risk, especially service and sales and clerical support.
Exposure is highest in NCR, where around two in five jobs are exposed. Central Luzon and Calabarzon both exceed 30 percent.
Across ASEAN the ILO estimates 22.9 percent of employment in 2025, nearly 80 million workers, has more than minimal exposure, yet finds little widespread disruption so far.

sgWageTrajectory.note: Two measured states, not a yearly series. The second is reported as a range, so it is drawn as a band rather than a line.

ebet.cap: Capped at the lower of 5 percent of total direct labour expenses or 25 million pesos a year.
ebet.note: An additional deduction from taxable income, equivalent to this share of actual training expenses.

journey.label: Role starts changing
journey.body: Parts of her role are automated. Her job is not removed, but the tasks she was hired for are shrinking. Philippine exposure is concentrated in exactly this kind of service and sales work.

journey.label: Referred, not released
journey.body: Her employer refers her to the PESO rather than ending the role. The PESO assesses her against conversion roles the sector is actually hiring for.

journey.label: Hired into the new role first
journey.body: She is taken on in the new role before she is fully trained. This is the step that makes it place-and-train rather than train-and-place.

journey.label: Trained inside the enterprise
journey.body: Training is delivered by the employer or with a technical-vocational institution, registered under the EBET framework, which already covers employed workers.

journey.label: Income continues
journey.body: A training allowance and stipend keep her earning during the conversion. This is the part that does not exist for mid-career workers today, and it is what the proposal would have to create.

journey.label: Measured, not assumed
journey.body: Completion, retention at six months and wage change are recorded, so the result is evidence rather than an expectation.

implActors.name: DOLE and the Bureau of Local Employment
implActors.statutory: Already administers JobStart nationwide under RA 10869, including the employer grant, the trainee allowance and monthly monitoring.
implActors.proposed: Would own the conversion track, set the income-support rule for mid-career trainees, and consolidate outcome reporting. That income-support rule does not exist today in any form.

implActors.name: Public Employment Service Offices
implActors.statutory: Already run JobStart intake, assessment and monthly monitoring at local level.
implActors.proposed: Would assess workers referred by automating employers and match them to conversion roles. No agency currently performs this matching function for displaced workers.

implActors.name: TESDA
implActors.statutory: Primary implementing agency for enterprise-based training under RA 12063, and accredits providers. Already opened more than 23,000 LinkedIn Learning courses to its stakeholders.
implActors.proposed: Would register conversion training under the EBET framework and tie registration to employer-confirmed roles, which answers the ADB finding that the most availed courses often lead to low-productivity occupations.

implActors.name: Participating employers
implActors.statutory: Under RA 12063 may deliver enterprise-based training alone or with a technical-vocational institution, and may claim the Section 20 training-expense deduction.
implActors.proposed: Would hire into the converted role before training completes, and report retention and wage outcomes. Hiring first is the assumption the whole model rests on, and no employer has agreed to it.

implActors.name: Training providers and TVIs
implActors.statutory: Deliver TESDA-accredited training, and may partner with enterprises under the EBET framework.
implActors.proposed: Would deliver courses mapped to confirmed conversion vacancies rather than to general course demand.

implActors.name: DICT and IBPAP
implActors.statutory: Already align programme strategies around the 740 million peso IT-BPM reskilling commitment targeting up to 340,000 participants.
implActors.proposed: Would identify which growth roles are worth converting into, and could fund a first cohort from the existing commitment rather than a new appropriation.

implActors.name: Local government units
implActors.statutory: Host and staff the PESO function.
implActors.proposed: Would carry the additional PESO workload the track creates. This is a real cost and is listed among the risks rather than assumed away.

implActors.name: Workers in exposed roles
implActors.proposed: Would take up a conversion place and complete the cycle. Worker acceptance is unmeasured in every source reviewed, which is why one SMART indicator sets a baseline rather than a pass mark.

risks.risk: Employers may not hire before training is complete
risks.why: The whole model fails without this
risks.mit: Start with IT-BPM firms already running AI pilots and already funding reskilling

risks.risk: No income-support rule exists for mid-career trainees
risks.why: RA 12063 covers training, not wages during conversion
risks.mit: Set the allowance by analogy to the JobStart stipend, which government already administers

risks.risk: Courses may not match real vacancies
risks.why: ADB found the most availed TVET courses often lead to low-productivity occupations
risks.mit: Tie programme registration to employer-confirmed conversion roles

risks.why: Different labour market, different wage structure
risks.mit: Treat the Philippine version as a pilot to be measured, not a promise

risks.why: A conversion track needs continuity to be worth building
risks.mit: Report results early enough to make the case for a standing line

risks.risk: Outcome data may not be obtainable
risks.why: Retention and wage measures depend on employer returns and record matching
risks.mit: Agree the data arrangement before the first cohort, not after
